title: Iris and the Wait Here Fiasco
markdown:
Iris the fox smoothed her tweed waistcoat in the Old Town Museum and called it comfort. Tonight was the first late opening, planned to the last label, and she was the archivist who had done the planning. Cases gleamed. A Roman glass had been turned a quarter-inch so the label agreed with the light. Director Albright, a badger with permanently surprised eyebrows, had a way of looking at her as if a rescue were already on the calendar. A tremor in her whiskers named the thing she would not say: that she might stumble in public and prove she was only a keeper of paper after all.

Jonah the pine marten bounced in the anteroom, tail ticking. "Ready for the big show?"

"As ready as I can be." Steady voice. Flutter underneath. She did not fear a clean failure so much as the particular heat of being saved in front of people who read plaques for fun.

Albright had boomed the rules before the doors, voice filling the marble as if marble needed instructions. Exhibits lit. Atmosphere hushed and respectful. For drinks and snacks, one sign: Please Wait Here For Service. Simple, he said, and looked at Iris as if simple were an exam. She, diligent past the point of mercy, took him at his letters.

Under lanterns the museum felt like a different building. Stone took a warm colour. Old paper and lemon polish. A new buzz, polite, expectant. This was public territory, a long walk from the quiet stacks where nobody queued for cheese. She straightened labels for the tenth time and then a leftover eleventh, because her paws wanted a job that could not go wrong.

Jonah was already at the refreshment station, frowning at his own handiwork as if it might confess. "Please Wait Here For Service. I've made sure everyone will wait right here." He pointed with pride at a spot that made architectural sense and culinary none.

The sign was clear, perfectly printed, and a good twenty paces from the pastry. Cheeses sat by the ancient urns like neglected ambassadors. A knot pulled in Iris's middle. She saw, too late, the line she had drawn between obedience and hunger. The archives offered their old invitation: freeze, fetch Albright, let the director be the adult in the room. She put the thought down and left it there, though it kept a chair.

Guests arrived, academics and art-lovers, footsteps polite on polish. A woman in pearls studied a label Iris had aligned with a ruler. Professor Eldridge came in with the air of a man who had seen worse lighting and survived. For a breath Iris felt the evening actually happening, a small bright accomplishment, doors open, plan in motion.

He noticed the queue almost at once: a confused cluster by the welcome desk, eyes making a pilgrimage toward distant tarts, nobody quite rude enough to defect. His chuckle carried, warm, fatal.

"Ah. The wait-here protocol. Clever. I assume the delicious part is over by the Etruscan urns?"

Amused glances travelled the hall like a draft. Someone whispered Etruscan as if it were a punchline. Iris's fur went hot. The pastries smelled like a joke at her expense, butter and apricot and the cost of taking a booming sentence too straight. Jonah caught her eye and nodded, small, as if she already knew the next line.

She did. The find was a working evening with a catch: everyone had come, and everyone was standing in the wrong country. The take, the effort she had not wanted, was to say so without a director attached.

"Professor Eldridge." Her voice held. Her heart did not. "Apologies. The sign was a little too brief. An archivist's conciseness, trying to obey the director, is a poor way to feed people. Please come to the table. We are ready to serve you now that anyone can see where."

A sigh of understanding, then delighted murmur. Jonah reached the station in a dash and began handing plates as if he had always lived there. The obedient cluster broke, reformed, and discovered cheese. Hushed reverence loosened into a friendly buzz. Real laughter found the high ceiling and liked it. A child was allowed a second pastry on the grounds of scholarship. Albright, watching the repair from a pillar, gave Iris a curt nod that might, if you were generous, have been respect.

Later the last guest went into the night with a napkin. Locket clasps clicked. Jonah grinned, tired in a good way. "Well. An event."

Iris found a crumb on her waistcoat and left it a moment, a small terrestrial exhibit, before brushing it off. The oak doors shuddered in a gust; she flinched, the old whisper, then stood the flinch up and put it away. The museum had been a set of rules with dust on. Tonight it had been a hall that could survive a sign in the wrong place, provided someone said so and moved the queue.
characters: Iris (fox museum archivist), Jonah (pine marten friend)
